item_description: A Greek hero of the Trojan War and central figure in Homer’s Iliad.
item_facts: Achilles is the central warrior in much of the Iliad.
The poem focuses on his anger during the Trojan War.
The story of his vulnerable heel is not told in the Iliad and comes from later traditions.
needs_review: Distinguish Homeric epic from later myth versions, especially the heel tradition.

item_description: A Greek goddess associated with love, beauty and desire.
item_facts: Aphrodite’s birth has different accounts in Greek myth.
She is associated with the Roman goddess Venus.
Her cult was important at sites including Cyprus and Cythera.
needs_review: Birth myths and cult traditions vary; verify against classical sources.

item_description: A Greek god associated with music, prophecy, healing, archery and light.
item_facts: Apollo was the son of Zeus and Leto in Greek myth.
His oracle at Delphi was among the ancient world’s most influential.
He is distinct from Helios, though later traditions sometimes associate them.
needs_review: Verify historical development of Apollo’s attributes and relationship with Helios.

item_description: The Greek god of war, often representing its violent and chaotic aspects.
item_facts: Ares is the son of Zeus and Hera in common genealogies.
He is associated with the Roman god Mars, though their cultural roles differ.
In Greek literature he is not always portrayed as victorious or respected.
needs_review: Avoid treating Roman and Greek war deities as identical; verify literary context.

item_description: A Greek goddess associated with hunting, wilderness and childbirth, and twin sister of Apollo.
item_facts: Artemis is commonly described as a daughter of Zeus and Leto.
She was associated with the protection of young people and wild animals.
Her cult and attributes differed among regions.
needs_review: Verify regional cult practices and varied roles using classical sources.

item_description: A Greek goddess of wisdom, strategic warfare and crafts, and patron of Athens.
item_facts: Athena was the daughter of Zeus in Greek myth.
The Parthenon in Athens was dedicated to Athena Parthenos.
She is often depicted with an owl, helmet and shield.
needs_review: Verify cult, temple and iconographic details through classical references.

item_description: The multi-headed hound that guards the entrance to the underworld in Greek mythology.
item_facts: Cerberus prevents the dead from leaving Hades in many accounts.
The number of heads varies across ancient sources and later retellings.
Heracles captures Cerberus as one of his labors.
needs_review: Head count varies in sources; avoid stating one version as universal.

item_description: A Greek goddess of agriculture and grain, whose myth explains the seasonal cycle through Persephone.
item_facts: Demeter is the mother of Persephone in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter.
The Eleusinian Mysteries were associated with Demeter and Persephone.
Her worship was connected with agriculture and fertility.
needs_review: Mystery-cult details are incomplete and debated; avoid claims about secret rites.

item_description: A Greek god associated with wine, theater, festivity and altered states.
item_facts: Dionysus was worshipped in festivals involving drama.
He is the son of Zeus in many traditions.
His myth includes travel, transformations and resistance to his worship.
needs_review: Dionysian cult and myth varied substantially by place and period.

item_description: The Greek god who rules the underworld and the realm of the dead.
item_facts: Hades is a brother of Zeus and Poseidon in Greek genealogies.
The underworld itself is also called Hades in English retellings.
He is distinct from Thanatos, the personification of death.
needs_review: Clarify deity versus place and check terminology against ancient sources.

item_description: The Greek god of smithing, metalwork, fire and skilled craftsmanship.
item_facts: Hephaestus made weapons and objects for gods in myth.
He was associated with volcanoes and the forge in later interpretations.
Stories of his parentage differ between sources.
needs_review: Parentage and myth details vary; distinguish ancient accounts.

item_description: Queen of the Olympian gods and a Greek goddess associated with marriage and family.
item_facts: Hera is the wife and sister of Zeus in Greek myth.
She was a major patron deity at Argos and Samos.
Her myths often involve conflict with Zeus’s lovers and children.
needs_review: Verify regional cult roles and avoid reducing Hera to a single mythic trait.

item_description: A Greek hero famous for completing a cycle of extraordinary labors; called Hercules in Roman tradition.
item_facts: Heracles was the son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene in a common account.
The Twelve Labors are central to his mythology.
His name and stories were adapted widely in Roman culture.
needs_review: Labors differ among sources; distinguish Greek Heracles from later Roman adaptations.

item_description: A Greek god who serves as messenger, guide of travelers and psychopomp for the dead.
item_facts: Hermes is a son of Zeus and Maia.
He is associated with trade, boundaries and communication.
His Roman counterpart is Mercury.
needs_review: Verify roles and regional variations through classical sources.

item_description: A Gorgon whose gaze turns people to stone in later versions of Greek myth.
item_facts: Medusa is the only mortal among the three Gorgons in some traditions.
Perseus kills her using a reflective shield in a well-known story.
Her origin and whether she was born monstrous or transformed vary across ancient accounts.
needs_review: The Ovid transformation story is later than Greek archaic sources; distinguish versions.

item_description: The Greek king of Ithaca whose difficult journey home after the Trojan War is told in the Odyssey.
item_facts: Odysseus is the central character of Homer’s Odyssey.
The poem describes a ten-year journey home after the war.
He is known for cunning, but portrayals differ across Greek literature.
needs_review: Distinguish epic narrative chronology from later retellings.

item_description: The winged horse of Greek mythology, most famously associated with the hero Bellerophon.
item_facts: Pegasus is born from Medusa’s blood after Perseus kills her in a common tradition.
Bellerophon rides Pegasus in the fight against the Chimera.
Later stories associate Pegasus with Zeus and the Muses.
needs_review: Pegasus traditions vary; verify birth and later associations across sources.

item_description: A Greek goddess who is queen of the underworld and daughter of Demeter.
item_facts: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter tells of her abduction by Hades.
Her return to the upper world is linked to the agricultural cycle in the hymn.
The length of her stay below differs among versions.
needs_review: Seasonal explanation differs among texts and interpretations; avoid a rigid universal version.

item_description: A Greek god of the sea, earthquakes and horses, and brother of Zeus and Hades.
item_facts: Poseidon was worshipped by seafarers and coastal communities.
He is associated with the trident in Greek art and literature.
His Roman counterpart is Neptune.
needs_review: Verify cult and attribute details with classical sources.

item_description: King of the Olympian gods in Greek mythology, associated with the sky, thunder and authority.
item_facts: Zeus is the son of Cronus and Rhea in standard Greek genealogies.
He overthrows the Titans in the Theogony of Hesiod.
His cult and titles differed among Greek communities.
needs_review: Verify genealogy and local variations; distinguish mythic sources.
